plain_english:
Before you start anything, think about what it will take and what could happen. Then decide. Otherwise you'll jump in full of energy, not thinking about the consequences. When things get tough, you'll quit in shame.

"I want to win at the Olympics." Fine. But think about what that means. If it's worth it, then commit. You'll have to follow strict rules. You'll eat a special diet and give up treats. You'll exercise your body at set times whether you feel like it or not, in heat and cold. You can't drink cold water. Sometimes no wine at all. You basically hand your life over to your trainer like a patient to a doctor. Then in the actual competition, you might get thrown in a ditch, dislocate your arm, twist your ankle, swallow tons of dust, get beaten for mistakes, and still lose.

Once you've counted up all of this, if you still want to do it, then go fight.
original_excerpt: In every affair consider what precedes and what follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit, indeed, careless of the consequences, and when these are developed, you will shamefully desist. "I would conquer at the Olympic Games." But consider what precedes and what follows, and then, if it be for your advantage, engage in the affair. You must conform to rules, submit to a diet, refrain from dainties; exercise your body, whether you choose it or not, at a stated hour, in heat and cold; you must drink no cold water, and sometimes no wine—in a word, you must give yourself up to your trainer as to a physician. Then, in the combat, you may be thrown into a ditch, dislocate your arm, turn your ankle, swallow an abundance of dust, receive stripes [for negligence], and, after all, lose the victory. When you have reckoned up all this, if your inclination still holds, set about the combat.

plain_english: Otherwise, here's what will happen. You'll act like children who play pretend. They see a wrestling match and suddenly they're wrestlers. They see gladiators and now they're gladiators. They hear a trumpet and they want to be musicians. They watch a play and they're actors. That's exactly what you'll do. One day you'll be a wrestler, the next a gladiator. Today a philosopher, tomorrow a public speaker. But you won't be serious about any of it. Like a monkey, you'll copy everything you see. You'll get excited about something new, then lose interest once the novelty wears off. Why? Because you never think things through. You don't examine what you're getting into or test whether it's right for you. You just jump in carelessly, with half-hearted effort.
original_excerpt: Otherwise, take notice, you will behave like children who sometimes play wrestlers, sometimes gladiators, sometimes blow a trumpet, and sometimes act a tragedy, when they happen to have seen and admired these shows. Thus you too will be at one time a wrestler, and another a gladiator; now a philosopher, now an orator; but nothing in earnest. Like an ape you mimic all you see, and one thing after another is sure to please you, but is out of favor as soon as it becomes familiar. For you have never entered upon anything considerately; nor after having surveyed and tested the whole matter, but carelessly, and with a halfway zeal.

plain_english: Some people hear a great philosopher speak—like Euphrates, though who could speak like him?—and suddenly want to become philosophers too. But first, consider what this actually involves. Ask yourself what your nature can handle. If you wanted to be a wrestler, you'd examine your shoulders, your back, your thighs. Different people are built for different things. Do you think you can keep living exactly as you do now and be a philosopher? Keep eating, drinking, getting angry, and complaining like before? You'll have to stay alert. You'll have to work hard. You'll have to control certain desires. You'll have to leave your friends behind. Your servant will look down on you. People you meet will laugh at you. You'll lose out to others in everything—jobs, honors, court cases. Think through all of this carefully. Then approach philosophy if you want—but only if you're willing to give up these things to gain peace of mind, freedom, and calm. If not, don't bother. Don't be like children who want to be a philosopher one day, a tax collector the next, then a public speaker, then one of Caesar's officers. These roles don't mix. You must be one person—either good or bad. Either develop your mind or chase external things. Focus on what's within you or what's outside you. Be either a philosopher or just another person in the crowd.
original_excerpt: Thus some, when they have seen a philosopher and heard a man speaking like Euphrates—though, indeed, who can speak like him?—have a mind to be philosophers, too. Consider first, man, what the matter is, and what your own nature is able to bear. If you would be a wrestler, consider your shoulders, your back, your thighs; for different persons are made for different things. Do you think that you can act as you do and be a philosopher, that you can eat, drink, be angry, be discontented, as you are now? You must watch, you must labor, you must get the better of certain appetites, must quit your acquaintances, be despised by your servant, be laughed at by those you meet; come off worse than others in everything—in offices, in honors, before tribunals. When you have fully considered all these things, approach, if you please—that is, if, by parting with them, you have a mind to purchase serenity, freedom, and tranquillity. If not, do not come hither; do not, like children, be now a philosopher, then a publican, then an orator, and then one of Caesar's officers. These things are not consistent. You must be one man, either good or bad. You must cultivate either your own reason or else externals; apply yourself either to things within or without you—that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.
